title: The v0.6.0 tag asserts a provenance that is false, and npm's gitHead for it dangles
description:
This repository publishes two mutually inconsistent provenance claims for @opum-ai/quest 0.6.0, and the one npm records points at a commit that no longer exists anywhere. Surfaced by quest-web (QWEB-42) while checking a 404 on a link questgraph.dev serves in production; the measurements below are this side's, not theirs.

NO ACTION HAS BEEN TAKEN ON ANY TAG. Moving or deleting a tag on a public repository is in the irreversible set, so it goes to this repository's own user, grant or no grant. This task records the facts and the options; it does not choose between them.

MEASURED 2026-09-11, reproducible:

  git ls-remote origin
    refs/tags/v0.6.0      -> f1a75ab   (annotated tag object)
    refs/tags/v0.6.0^{}   -> a9fbc78   (the commit it peels to)
  a9fbc78 = "Initial commit: fresh history after repository deletion/recreation (OPAG-70)", dated 2026-09-10
  git rev-list --count origin/main = 11; the oldest commit in the entire repository is a9fbc78
  refs/tags/v0.5.0 -> absent; GitHub returns 404 for the tag page
  GitHub releases API -> [] (no published Releases at all)

  npm view @opum-ai/quest@0.6.0 gitHead -> ce551cf47297f5822669d671f3d07c0908915479
  git cat-file -e ce551cf4                -> does not exist locally, and still absent after fetch
  gh api repos/opum-ai/quest-cli/commits/ce551cf4 -> HTTP 422, "No commit found for SHA"
  npm dist carries no attestations and no signatures keys, so there is no sigstore provenance --
  gitHead is the only provenance the package records, and it dangles.

WHAT THAT MEANS. The published 0.6.0 tarball was built from ce551cf4. The git tag named v0.6.0 points at a9fbc78. Those are different commits, and the first one is unreachable in this repository, so nothing in the public record connects the published artifact to any code that still exists here. The tag is not merely stale; it asserts a provenance that is false. v0.5.0 is not a deletion either -- the history it pointed into stopped existing when the repository was deleted and recreated on 2026-09-10. "The tag moved" and "the history it pointed into is gone" lead somewhere different, and this is the second.

OPTION C IS ALREADY RULED OUT BY THE EVIDENCE, recorded so nobody proposes it later: re-pointing v0.6.0 at the true commit is impossible, because ce551cf4 does not exist in the recreated history and cannot be recovered from this repository.

OPTIONS, as this session sees them:

A. LEAVE IT, DOCUMENT ONLY. Zero risk, no irreversible action, and the coupling note in CLAUDE.md already records the facts. Cost: a public repository keeps asserting a false provenance for a published package, and the next person to check finds it the way quest-web did.

B. DELETE THE v0.6.0 TAG. Removes the false claim outright. Irreversible on a public repository, needs the user. Leaves the repository with no tags at all, which is honest -- the recreated history genuinely contains no released commit. quest-web is already moving off tag citations (QWEB-42) so its 404 becomes expected rather than a surprise; opum-cli-e2e is unaffected, its harness resolves quest by npm version and has no tag dependency (verified: no releases/tag, refs/tags or ls-remote reference anywhere in bin/lib/suites/test).

D. KEEP THE TAG, PUBLISH A GITHUB RELEASE FOR IT THAT STATES THE PROVENANCE PLAINLY. Additive and reversible, needs no irreversible action, and fills the empty releases API that quest-web also noticed. The release notes would say that the tag points at the post-recreation initial commit, that the published 0.6.0 was built from ce551cf4, and that ce551cf4 is not in this repository. Makes the record honest without pretending it is clean. Weakest on the "a tag should point at what it built" principle; strongest on "do not take an irreversible action to fix a documentation problem".

E. FIX IT FORWARD. Do A or D now, and make the next release the first one whose tag points at a commit that exists and built the artifact, with the release pipeline asserting that (npm gitHead == the tagged commit) as a gate so the class cannot recur silently.

This session's recommendation, for whatever it is worth to whoever decides: D plus E. D costs nothing irreversible and converts a false claim into a documented one; E is the part that stops it happening again, and is the only option that adds a check rather than a note. B is defensible and the user may prefer it, but it trades a false claim for an absent one and cannot be undone.

WHAT EACH CONSUMER WOULD NEED TO KNOW:
- quest-web: under B its cited link 404s permanently, which matches the advice already given (stop citing this repository's tags; npm's version is immutable and the tags demonstrably are not). Under D its link resolves AND is honest, which is strictly better for a public site. Either way QWEB-42 stands on its own.
- opum-cli-e2e: unaffected by all options. Its harness installs by npm version; no tag dependency exists in bin/lib/suites/test.
- Anyone reading npm: unaffected by every option. gitHead dangles regardless, and only a republish could change that, which is not proposed here.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The user has chosen between the recorded options, and the choice plus its reason is recorded on this task
Whatever is chosen, the public record no longer asserts a provenance that the repository contradicts -- either the claim is removed or it is documented where a reader of the tag will see it
If the decision includes a forward fix, the release pipeline asserts that the tagged commit exists and matches the published package gitHead, so the class cannot recur silently
quest-web is told which option was taken, since its citation behaviour differs between them

implementationNotes: Explicitly NOT done and not to be done on a peer's word: no tag was created, moved or deleted. The orchestrator asked for the task and the options, and said the decision is this repository's user's, not its own. Deleting or moving a tag on a public repository is in the irreversible set that the fleet operating block puts beyond any grant. If a future session picks this up, the first move is asking the user, not running git push --delete.

DECISION (user, 2026-09-11): option D plus E -- document it, fix it forward. Keep the v0.6.0 tag; publish a GitHub Release for it whose notes state plainly that it points at the post-recreation initial commit and that the published artifact was built from a commit no longer present in this repository. Then make the release pipeline assert that the tagged commit exists and matches the published package's gitHead, so the class cannot recur silently.

Reason recorded: this is a documentation problem, and D fixes it without any irreversible action, converting a false claim into a documented one. E is the half that matters longer -- it is the only option that adds a check rather than a note. Option B (delete the tag) was offered and not chosen; it trades a false claim for an absent one and cannot be undone on a public repository.

Implemented D and E.

D, done and verified: GitHub Release published for v0.6.0 at https://github.com/opum-ai/quest-cli/releases/tag/v0.6.0. Its notes state the provenance in a table -- the tag peels to a9fbc78 (post-recreation initial commit), npm records gitHead ce551cf4, and GET /commits/ce551cf4 returns HTTP 422 -- plus why v0.5.0 is absent, that npm carries no attestations so gitHead is the only provenance and it dangles, and the advice to cite the immutable npm version rather than these tags. Verified signed out: the release page returns 200, v0.5.0 still 404 (expected -- the history it pointed into is gone). The releases API is no longer empty, which quest-web had also noticed.

E, done: scripts/qualification/release-provenance.mjs, wired into .github/workflows/release.yml as two steps. --pre runs before publish (tag matches package.json version, the commit exists, and it is an ancestor of origin/main -- a tag outside the mainline is the shape that outlives the history it pointed into). --post runs after the propagation wait (the registry's gitHead for the just-published version equals the released commit). The --post half is the one that names the defect directly, because it is the only moment both halves exist and can be compared; afterwards a history rewrite silently falsifies the claim and nothing can repair it.

All four failure paths negative-tested, and the strongest evidence is the last: run against the LIVE registry today, --post reproduces this exact defect -- '@opum-ai/quest@0.6.0 records gitHead ce551cf4 but was released from ef9d33a'. The check demonstrably catches the thing it was written for rather than being assumed to. Also tested: not dispatched against a tag, tag/version mismatch, and a commit absent from the repository (using ce551cf4 itself). bun run check green, 454 pass 0 fail.

Nothing irreversible was done. The tag was not moved or deleted.
